prompt: 10% of your service's request handling runs under one global mutex; the rest is perfectly parallel. Ignoring other overheads, what is the best possible speed-up on 16 cores compared with 1?

options.explanation: That assumes everything parallelises. The 10% under the lock runs one thread at a time no matter how many cores you add.
10× is the limit with *infinite* cores (1 / 0.1). With 16 cores the parallel part still takes 0.9/16 of the original time.
This underestimates badly; it would mean the lock serialised far more than 10% of the work.

workedExample:
Amdahl's law gives the best possible speed-up when part of the work can only run on one core at a time:

```formula
S(N) = 1 / (s + p / N)
S(16) = 1 / (0.10 + 0.90 / 16)
S(16) = 1 / (0.10 + 0.05625)
S(16) = 1 / 0.15625 = 6.4
where
S(N): the speed-up on N cores, a plain ratio: how many times faster than on 1 core
s: the serial fraction, the share of time spent under the global lock: 0.10
p: the parallel fraction, 1 − s: 0.90
N: the number of cores: 16
In words: the locked tenth still runs one thread at a time, so 16 cores give only 6.4 times the speed.
```

Two follow-ups show where the limit lies:

```formula
S_max = 1 / s = 1 / 0.1 = 10
S(16) = 1 / (0.05 + 0.95 / 16) ≈ 9.1
where
S_max: the speed-up with unlimited cores, where the parallel part shrinks to nothing
S(16): the 16-core speed-up after halving the locked share to s = 0.05
s: the serial fraction
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: even infinite cores cannot beat 10 times here, but halving the locked share lifts 16 cores from 6.4 to about 9.1 times.
```

That is why shrinking critical sections matters so much.
